62. Radium Girls

During World War I, as men were drafted into service, women wanted to contribute with patriotism and by assuming greater responsibility, taking up factory work to support the war effort. Among these roles was the task of painting watch dials with radium, a luminescent substance celebrated for its supposed health benefits and used in products ranging from cosmetics to toothpaste, supposedly curing ailments and reversing ageing. The Radium Girls, employed by the United States Radium Corporation (USRC), revealed a grave injustice with corporate gaslighting and negligence.

At the time, wristwatches were only worn by women and homosexual men. However, the battlefield rendered pocket watches cumbersome for soldiers and using matches to check the time risked revealing the location of trenches. Radium offered a solution: painting watch dials with radium-based paint, branded as 'Undark', enabled visibility in the dark. The USRC, a major defence contractor, supplied millions of these radioluminescent watches to both military personnel and civilians, employing approximately 300 workers, predominantly women, at its New Jersey plant.

Dial painting was perceived as glamorous. The women, paid three times the average factory wage, worked in sunlit studios, often wearing party dresses to let the radium powder make them glow, earning the nickname 'ghost girls'. They socialised and ate at radium-covered desks, playfully applying the paint to their nails, teeth and faces. Unbeknownst to them, this paint was deadly. While USRC owners and scientists, aware of the dangers of radium, used lead aprons, tongs and masks for protection, the company failed to inform its workers. Literature distributed to the medical community by USRC acknowledged the injurious effects of this chemical, yet workers were encouraged to use a "lip, dip, paint" technique, sharpening brushes with their lips and repeating the process up to a thousand times daily.

The consequences were catastrophic. Dentists first noted alarming symptoms among the dial painters: dental pain, loose teeth, ulcers and unhealing lesions. Many developed anaemia, bone fractures and a condition now known as radium jaw, characterised by jawbone necrosis. Some experienced suppressed menstruation, sterility and cancer. One of the earliest cases involved a worker whose toothache led to an extraction that would not heal. Her condition worsened with ulcers, lesions and a foul odour, rendering eating impossible and speech unbearable. Her jawbone disintegrated and she suffered excruciating pain until her jugular vein, affected by necrosis, caused her to haemorrhage to death. Even after exhumation, her bones glowed, a haunting testament to the impact of radium.

Initially, doctors attributed her death to syphilis, a diagnosis that deflected blame from USRC and brought shame to her family, given the stigma of the era. As more women fell ill with similar symptoms, USRC denied any connection to their work for two years. Facing public scrutiny and declining business, the company commissioned an independent study, which confirmed radium exposure as the cause of death. However, USRC rejected these findings, funding additional studies that falsely exonerated them and vilifying the afflicted workers. Public perception of the health benefits and safety of radium persisted, despite the mounting evidence. 

The irony of the tragedy lies in its avoidability. In Europe, similar dial-painting work was conducted without allowing workers to place radium near their mouths, a practice USRC actively taught in the training. The suffering of the Radium Girls, fighting the system on their deathbeds, exposed not only corporate malfeasance but also a broader failure to prioritise worker safety. Their ordeal, marked by pain, destruction of reputation and betrayal, underscores the devastating consequences of prioritising profit over human lives, cementing their legacy as a poignant reminder of the need for accountability and workplace protections. Where else have we seen this type of gaslighting?
